extraction_text: The fierce battle between the Pandavas and Kauravas is about to begin. The Pandava brothers, of great soul, take their seats.

attributes.context: Setting the stage for the main conflict

extraction_text: Balarama (Rama), whose emblem is the palmyra tree and weapon is the plough, hears a battle is about to begin between his two disciples and arrives at the site.

attributes.reason: To witness the battle between his disciples

extraction_text: The kings (lords) are overjoyed to see Balarama arrive. They pay him homage and request him to watch the skilled martial arts of his two disciples.

Balarama addresses Krishna, the son of Pandu (Arjuna), and Duryodhana of the Kuru clan, who stands holding a mace. He states he left 42 days ago under the constellation Ashvini and has returned under the constellation Bharani. He, a descendant of Madhu (Krishna), has come to watch the mace-fight of his two disciples.

attributes.relationship: Balarama as teacher to Krishna and Duryodhana

extraction_text: King Yudhishthira embraces Balarama, the plough-wielder, greets him according to custom, inquires after his health, and welcomes him.
The two famous dark-skinned great archers (Krishna and Arjuna) also greet Balarama with affection and joy, embracing him.
The two heroic sons of Madri (Nakula and Sahadeva) and the five sons of Draupadi stand up and pay homage to the mighty son of Rohini (Balarama).
The immensely powerful Bhima and your son (Duryodhana) also each hold their maces and duly worship the mighty one (Balarama).

attributes.context: Both combatants show respect before battle

extraction_text: The other kings also repeatedly salute and welcome Balarama, and say to the great-souled son of Rohini: 'O mighty-armed one, please watch this battle.'
The energetic Balarama embraces the sons of Pandu and the Srinjayas, and inquires after the health of all the Pandavas. They, in turn, approach, return the greetings, and ask after his well-being.
The high-minded plough-wielder (Balarama) praises the Kshatriyas and greets them one by one according to their age.

attributes.relationship: Balarama showing respect to the assembly

extraction_text: He embraces Janardana (Krishna) and Satyaki with affection, smells their heads, and inquires after their health.

attributes.relationship: Especially close bond with Krishna (his brother) and Satyaki

extraction_text: They (Krishna and Satyaki) also, filled with delight, duly worship their teacher, just as Indra and Indra's younger brother (Vishnu) worship the lord of the gods, Brahma.

attributes.relationship: Balarama as revered teacher, compared to divine hierarchy

extraction_text: The son of Dharma (Yudhishthira) says to the victorious son of Rohini (Balarama): 'O Rama, please watch this great battle between brothers!'

attributes.context: Highlights the fratricidal nature of the battle

extraction_text: The auspicious, mighty-armed hero, the elder brother of the beautiful-haired one (Krishna), happily takes his seat amidst everyone, attended upon respectfully by the chariot warriors.
He, dressed in dark blue garments, sits resplendent among the kings, like the moon in the sky surrounded by stars.
Thus, to settle the enmity between your two descendants (the Pandavas and Kauravas), a hair-raising, cruel combat is about to begin.
Narrator (Janamejaya) states: Initially, on the eve of the great war, Balarama left the battlefield with many Vrishnis.

attributes.context: Historical note explaining his absence until now

extraction_text: Balarama (Rama) declares his neutrality in the Kurukshetra War, stating he will neither help the Kauravas (Duryodhana's side) nor the Pandavas, and departs to go where he wishes.

relationships: Neutral to both Kauravas and Pandavas

extraction_text: After settling in Upaplavya, the Pandavas send Krishna as an envoy to Dhritarashtra in Hastinapura to seek peace for everyone's benefit.
Dhritarashtra refuses to listen to Krishna's peace proposal, causing the mission to fail.

relationships: Conflict between Kauravas and Pandavas escalates

extraction_text: Krishna returns to Upaplavya and informs the Pandavas of the failed mission, telling them to prepare for battle on the day of the constellation Punarvasu.

attributes.action: Report of failed peace and preparation for war

extraction_text: When armies are arrayed for battle, Balarama (son of Rohini) suggests to his brother Krishna that they should help in the war, but Krishna does not listen to him.

attributes.action: Suggestion to participate in war, rejected

extraction_text: Balarama, displeased with Krishna's decision, departs on a pilgrimage to the Sarasvati River on the day of the constellation Revati, accompanied by all the Yadava people.
Balarama instructs his attendants to bring all pilgrimage necessities, sacred fires, priests, wealth, animals, vehicles, and provisions for the journey to the Sarasvati River.

relationships: Balarama as leader organizing the expedition

extraction_text: Balarama sets out on the pilgrimage from the sea toward the Sarasvati River as the Kuru clan engages in mutual slaughter (the Kurukshetra War begins).
During their journey, Balarama and his companions distribute prepared food to the weary, weak, children, elderly, and hungry people along the way.
King Janamejaya (镇群) asks Vaishampayana (护民子) to describe the characteristics, origins, merits, and rituals of the sacred sites along the Sarasvati River.
Vaishampayana begins describing the journey of Balarama (罗摩) along the Sarasvati River, where he generously gives gifts to Brahmins at sacred sites.

supernatural_elements: Balarama is described as a Yadava hero with great soul

extraction_text: Balarama gives thousands of gold-horned milk cows, horses, chariots, female slaves, jewels, pearls, corals, gold ornaments, silver, and metal vessels to Brahmins.
Balarama travels to various sacred sites along the Sarasvati River and eventually arrives at Kurukshetra.
Vaishampayana starts describing the first sacred site, Prabhasa, where the Moon (众星之王) once suffered from consumption and was cured after bathing there.

relationships: Moon is the subject of the story
supernatural_elements: Moon is cured by bathing in Prabhasa

extraction_text: King Janamejaya asks why the Moon suffered from consumption, how it came to bathe at Prabhasa, and how it recovered.
Vaishampayana begins explaining that Daksha (陀刹) had twenty-seven daughters whom he married to the Moon.

relationships: Moon is husband to twenty-seven daughters
supernatural_elements: Moon marrying twenty-seven daughters sets up mythological context

extraction_text: The moon god Chandra's wives, the Nakshatras (constellations), became dissatisfied because Chandra exclusively favored his wife Rohini over them.

attributes.relationships: Chandra is husband to Rohini and the Nakshatras. Rohini is his favorite wife.

extraction_text: The Nakshatras returned to their father, Prajapati Daksha, to complain about Chandra's favoritism.

attributes.relationships: Prajapati Daksha is the father of the Nakshatras.

extraction_text: Prajapati Daksha instructed Chandra to treat all his wives equally and warned him against violating dharma.
Chandra ignored Daksha's warning and continued to favor only Rohini.
The Nakshatras returned to Daksha a second time, stating Chandra was disregarding his command.
Prajapati Daksha warned Chandra again to treat his wives equally, this time threatening a curse.
Chandra continued to ignore the warning, favoring only Rohini, which angered the other wives.
The Nakshatras returned to Daksha a third time, seeking his protection.

attributes.action: Third complaint and plea for protection

extraction_text: Prajapati Daksha, angered by Chandra's continued defiance, cursed Chandra with consumption (tuberculosis), causing him to waste away.
Chandra tried various remedies and performed sacrifices but could not cure the curse, continuing to waste away.
As Chandra wasted away, herbs began to wither and lose their potency, endangering all life.
The gods visited Chandra to inquire about his condition and the cause of his suffering.
The gods inquired about the cause of Moon's (Soma/Chandra) affliction, and he revealed he was suffering from consumption due to a curse.
The gods went to Daksha and pleaded with him to revoke the curse on Moon, explaining the widespread negative effects on the world.

attributes.reason: Moon's wasting affects all beings, plants, and even the gods

extraction_text: Daksha declared his spoken words could not be retracted but offered a mitigation: Moon must treat all his wives equally and bathe in the sacred site on the Sarasvati River to gradually recover.

attributes.condition: Equal treatment of wives and ritual bathing

extraction_text: Daksha further decreed that Moon would wane for half a month and wax for the other half henceforth.
Moon went to the sacred site Prabhasa on the Sarasvati River, bathed on the new moon night, and regained his cool radiance, illuminating the world.

attributes.result: Moon's recovery and return of light

extraction_text: The gods accompanied Moon back to Daksha, who received them and advised Moon never to disrespect women or Brahmins, urging self-restraint.

attributes.moral_instruction: Respect for women and Brahmins, self-discipline

extraction_text: Moon returned to his abode, and all beings rejoiced, resuming their normal lives; the story explains the origin of Prabhasa's fame and the lunar cycle.

attributes.action: Return and restoration of cosmic order
attributes.result: Universal happiness and established lunar phases

extraction_text: The hero Rama (Balarama) proceeded to the sacred site Cup-spring, performed charitable acts, bathed, and gained merit before moving to Uddapana.

attributes.result: Acquisition of good fortune and merit

extraction_text: At Uddapana, sages inferred the Sarasvati River flows underground due to the moist land and vegetation.
